questions.prompt: In `Merge`, `i` and `j` start at `0`, but the write index `k` starts at `left`. Why?
options: Because `left` is always `0` on the first call
So the merge runs from right to left, which keeps it stable
Because the merged values must go back into this subarray's slice of the original array; starting at `0` would overwrite other elements
questions.explanation: `i` and `j` index the temporary `leftArr` and `rightArr`, which start at 0. `k` writes into the original array, so it must start where the current subarray starts.

questions.prompt: With `left = 0` and `mid = 2`, which elements of `arr` does `arr[left..(mid + 1)]` copy into `leftArr`?
questions.explanation: In C# range syntax the start index is inclusive and the end index is exclusive, so `arr[0..3]` contains indexes 0, 1 and 2, that is `left` through `mid`.

questions.prompt: `Partition(arr, 0, 6)` is called on the sorted array `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]`. What does it return?
questions.explanation: The pivot `7` is the largest value, so every other element is `<= pivot` and `i` ends at 5. The pivot stays at index 6, leaving 6 elements on the left and none on the right.

questions.prompt: Why does quicksort with a last-element pivot take O(n²) on an already sorted array?
options: Partitioning needs an extra O(n) array on each call
Sorted input makes every comparison swap two elements
The recursion stops early and the remaining elements are sorted by bubble sort
Each partition peels off only the pivot, so the recursion is `n` levels deep and each level still scans the remaining elements
questions.explanation: The split is `n-1` and `0` every time, so the tree has height `n` instead of `log n`, and the comparisons add up to `(n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2`.

questions.prompt: How do real-world quicksort implementations avoid the sorted-input worst case, and how does that compare with merge sort?
options: They sort the input first; after that both algorithms are guaranteed O(n log n)
They pick the pivot randomly or by median-of-three; merge sort guarantees O(n log n) on any input, while quicksort's average depends on the pivot choice
They always pick the first element instead of the last; merge sort has the same worst case
They switch to merge sort for any array larger than 32 elements
questions.explanation: Random or median-of-three pivots make the pathological pattern very unlikely, bringing quicksort back to O(n log n) on average. Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) regardless of input.
